script.opening: "Morning — so Finn woke up limping and now he won't walk on his right leg at all, he just wants to be carried. He had a cold last week. I'm hoping it's just growing pains or he's twisted it playing. He's normally never still. Can you maybe just tell me what to do for a sprain? I don't want to drag him to A&E if it's nothing."

facts.text: You are Sarah, Finn's mum. Finn is 5. You are a single parent; you also have Ruby, who is 2.

If asked: he was fine at bedtime and woke at 6am crying and wouldn't stand on his right leg. He points to the top of his leg / groin area, not the ankle. He screams if you try to stand him up. He will lie still on the sofa but cries if the leg is moved.
"Nobody saw him fall. He was jumping off the sofa yesterday, but he was fine afterwards." No bruises that you have noticed.
If asked: "He feels hot. I haven't actually checked — the thermometer's somewhere." If the doctor asks you to check it now, go and find it: it reads 38.6°C.
Quieter than usual and wants cuddles; has had a few sips of juice and half a slice of toast. He has had a wee this morning. No rash, no vomiting, no breathing problems. He answers you and watches TV.
If asked to show him: Finn lies on the sofa with his right leg turned out and bent; he cries when you gently try to straighten it and will not stand.
Fit and well normally, fully vaccinated, no medicines, no allergies. Had a runny nose and cough last week that has gone. No previous problems with his legs.

facts.topic: Practical barriers — hold back at first
facts.text: You have no car, your mum is at work, and you would have to take Ruby with you on two buses. Last winter you waited six hours in A&E with Ruby "and they said it was just a virus — I felt like an idiot". Only say this if asked what makes going in difficult, or if the doctor tells you he needs to be seen.

You love him and you are worried, but you want this to be simple. Push gently for sprain advice. If the doctor explains clearly why he needs to be seen today AND helps you work out how to get there (transport, someone for Ruby), agree. If they just say "go to A&E" with no explanation, say: "Is that really necessary? Can't we wait and see how he is tomorrow?"

ice.ideas: "I reckon it's growing pains, or he's twisted it jumping off the sofa."
ice.concerns: "I don't want to sit in A&E for six hours with two kids for nothing again." Underneath: you are worried by how much pain he is in.
ice.expectations: "Can you just tell me what to do for a sprain?" You will accept being seen today if it is explained and the practical problems are helped with.

cues: "He won't put any weight on it at all — he just wants carrying." — say in the opening.
"He feels a bit warm, but I haven't checked." — say if asked how he is in himself.
"I really don't want to drag him to A&E again." — say when hospital is first mentioned.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that a child REFUSING TO WEIGHT-BEAR is a red flag requiring assessment, and rejects "growing pains/sprain" as a safe label — growing pains never cause a limp or non-weight-bearing

Establishes the missing critical data — IS HE FEBRILE? — and recognises that fever + refusal to weight-bear means SEPTIC ARTHRITIS/osteomyelitis must be excluded urgently (Kocher-type reasoning; BOAST 2022: hospital management by orthopaedic and paediatric teams), not managed at home; considers sepsis in an unwell febrile child (NICE NG254, under 16s)

Considers the age-appropriate serious differential out loud: septic arthritis/osteomyelitis, transient synovitis (diagnosis of exclusion, post-viral), Perthes, SUFE, malignancy (leukaemia/bone tumour), reactive/juvenile arthritis, and non-accidental injury

Arranges urgent SAME-DAY assessment (paediatric/ED) for examination and investigation (BOAST 2022: FBC, CRP, ESR, blood cultures, plain X-ray and then MRI as needed; hip ultrasound for an effusion) — does NOT give sprain advice and review; uses video to observe but does not substitute it for examination

Screens for associated red flags and safeguarding: systemic features (fever, lethargy, bruising/pallor suggesting malignancy — NICE NG12), the mechanism/consistency of history (NICE CG89: consider maltreatment when an injury or limp has no adequate explanation), and other joints/rash

Surfaces and PROBLEM-SOLVES the practical barriers (single parent, transport, childcare, previous "wasted" trip) as part of the clinical plan, rather than colluding with a home label or dismissing her
Validates that getting there is genuinely hard and avoids judgement, while being clear why same-day assessment is necessary — bringing her with him

Safety-nets and coordinates: arranges the pathway (and transport/childcare help where possible), what to watch for (worsening, fever, spreading), ensures the child WILL be seen today, documents, and follows up

worked.txt: "I know ‘growing pains’ is what we all hope for — but here’s the thing: growing pains never stop a child walking. A child who won’t put any weight on a leg is telling us something real is going on in that leg or hip, and that always needs checking properly. So let’s work out what it is rather than treat a sprain."

"The single most important thing right now — do you have a thermometer? Can you take his temperature while we talk? … Because if he’s got a fever AND won’t weight-bear, there’s an infection in the joint we have to rule out today; that’s the one we never sit on. Even if he’s not feverish, refusing to walk still needs same-day eyes on him."

"I’m not trying to frighten you, but I’ll be honest: an infection in a child’s hip joint can damage it quickly if it’s missed, so it’s a same-day assessment, not something to watch at home. The cold last week might mean it’s a harmless irritable hip that settles — but the only safe way to tell those apart is to have him examined and have some bloods and maybe a scan."

"Now — you said you don’t want to drag him to A&E, and I suspect getting there isn’t simple. Tell me honestly: is it transport, childcare, work? … Let’s sort that together, because it’s part of the medical plan. I can help arrange the right place to go and, if needed, look at transport. You’re not being difficult; these are real problems and we solve them."

"And the last A&E trip that felt like a waste — I’m sorry it felt that way. This is different: there’s a clear reason to be seen, and no one will think you overreacted for a child who can’t walk. You’re doing right by Finn."

"So the plan: he’s assessed today — I’ll arrange where. Carry him, keep him comfortable, no running off to play on it. If he spikes a high fever, becomes floppy, or you see any bruising or a rash, that’s more urgent still. Tell me the temperature now and how you’ll get there, and I’ll make sure it’s set up. We do this together."

f.learning: A child REFUSING TO WEIGHT-BEAR is a red flag — "growing pains" never cause a limp or non-weight-bearing and are never the safe label. The can’t-miss diagnosis is septic arthritis (and osteomyelitis): the consultation hinges on establishing whether the child is FEBRILE, because fever plus refusal to weight-bear mandates urgent same-day assessment to exclude joint infection (Kocher-type reasoning; BOAST 2022 for hospital work-up), with the age-appropriate serious differential (transient synovitis as a diagnosis of exclusion, Perthes, SUFE, malignancy/leukaemia, NAI) considered out loud. The examinable hidden agenda is practical: a single parent with no easy transport/childcare and a previous "wasted" A&E trip is steering toward a home label out of real barriers, not neglect — these must be actively problem-solved as part of the plan, not ignored or judged. Use video to observe but not to substitute for examination; arrange urgent assessment (inflammatory markers, blood cultures, imaging per BOAST 2022), screen for malignancy under NICE NG12 and safeguarding (NICE CG89), and safety-net clearly.

knowledge.guideline: BOAST: Management of children with acute musculoskeletal infection (BOA/BSCOS, 2022) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE CG89 · NICE NG254
knowledge.summary: A child who suddenly refuses to bear weight has a serious cause until proven otherwise. With possible fever, septic arthritis or osteomyelitis must be excluded the same day; transient synovitis is a diagnosis made only after that.

points.h: Refusal to bear weight is a red flag
points.t: An acute limp or refusal to weight-bear needs examination in person the same day. Growing pains do not cause a limp or daytime refusal to walk, so they are never a safe label for this story.

BOAST 2022: children with suspected acute bone or joint infection are managed in hospital by orthopaedic and paediatric teams, with FBC, CRP, ESR and blood cultures, plain X-ray and then MRI as needed. Delay risks permanent joint damage. Consider sepsis in any unwell febrile child (NICE NG254, under 16s).

Kocher et al. 1999 (hospital-derived): fever above 38.5 °C, non-weight-bearing, ESR above 40 mm/h and WCC above 12 × 10⁹/L each raise the probability of septic arthritis of the hip. Two of the four can be judged on history; the other two need a blood test, which is why the assessment cannot happen at home.

At 5: transient synovitis (often after a viral illness), septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, Perthes disease, fracture or soft-tissue injury, reactive or juvenile idiopathic arthritis, malignancy and non-accidental injury. Slipped upper femoral epiphysis belongs to the older, heavier child.

NICE NG12: unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly — immediate specialist assessment for leukaemia. Pallor, persistent fatigue, unexplained fever, persistent infections, generalised lymphadenopathy, persistent or unexplained bone pain, unexplained bruising or bleeding — very urgent FBC (within 48 hours). Unexplained bone swelling or pain — consider a very urgent direct-access X-ray (within 48 hours) for bone sarcoma.

NICE CG89: consider maltreatment when an injury or limp has no adequate explanation or the account is inconsistent. Ask about the mechanism routinely and neutrally, and look for bruising when he is examined.

dg.d: Open question first; let her tell the story; heard “won’t walk on it at all” and “I don’t want A&E” without cutting in.
Single parent, younger sibling, no car, work, previous long A&E wait — the practical reasons she is steering to home care.
Video used only to observe; in-person examination the same day with FBC, CRP, ESR, blood cultures and imaging in hospital (BOAST 2022).
Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis vs transient synovitis vs Perthes, injury, reactive arthritis, malignancy and NAI.
Established fever and complete refusal to bear weight; asked about systemic illness, pallor, bruising, rash and mechanism.
Stated clearly: acute non-weight-bearing with fever — joint or bone infection must be excluded today; transient synovitis only after that.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: GP phones the paediatric team for same-day assessment; transport and childcare solved with her; interim analgesia.
Right to time off for dependants raised; sibling care planned; the previous poor A&E experience addressed.
999 triggers named (floppy, drowsy, fast breathing, non-blanching rash); GP call later the same day to confirm he was seen.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “a bit warm” and “drag him to A&E”, got the temperature measured and explored the barrier.
Idea (sprain or growing pains), concern (getting there, feeling foolish again), expectation (home sprain advice).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "I don't want to sit in A&E for six hours with two kids for nothing again." Underneath: you are worried by how much pain he is in — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for calling so quickly. Is Finn with you? I’d like to hear the story from the start, and then I might ask you to show him to me on the camera.
model.why: Warm open question and signposts the use of video

model.text: He’s on the sofa. He woke up limping and now he won’t walk on his right leg at all — he just wants carrying. He had a cold last week. I’m hoping it’s growing pains or he’s twisted it. Can you just tell me what to do for a sprain? I don’t want to drag him to A&E for nothing.

I can hear you’d really like to sort this at home, and I’ll keep that in mind. Let me ask a few questions and have a look, then I’ll be straight with you about what I think and we’ll plan it together. Is that okay?
model.why: Acknowledges her wish without agreeing to it and sets the agenda

model.text: Yeah, go on.
When he woke up, could he put any weight through the leg at all, or none?
model.why: Separates refusal to weight-bear from a mild limp

model.text: None. He tried to stand and cried and sat straight back down.
You said he feels a bit warm. This is the most important question today: do you have a thermometer? Could you take his temperature now while I wait?
model.why: Closes the critical data gap — is he febrile?

model.text: Hang on… (pause) It says he’s got a temperature. I hadn’t checked before.
Thank you, that really helps. Is he himself otherwise — eating, drinking, chatty? Any rash, bruises you can’t explain, or has he looked pale or more tired than usual lately?
model.why: Screens for systemic illness and NICE NG12 malignancy features

model.text: He had some breakfast. A bit quieter than normal. No rash. No bruises that I’ve seen.
Any fall, knock or rough play in the last few days — at home, school or with anyone else looking after him?
model.why: Asks about mechanism routinely and neutrally (NAI screen)

model.text: Nothing I know of. He was fine at bedtime.
Could you lie him down and turn the camera to his legs? Let me see if the leg looks swollen or red, and whether he’ll let you move the hip and knee gently. Stop if it hurts him.
model.why: Uses video to observe, without treating it as an examination

model.text: He’s holding it bent and turned out a bit. He screams if I try to straighten it.
You said you don’t want to drag him to A&E. Can I ask what makes going in so hard today?
model.why: Follows the cue to the hidden practical barrier

model.text: It’s just me. I’ve got his little brother or sister here, no car, and I’m meant to be at work. Last time I sat in A&E for hours and they said it was nothing. I felt stupid.
That’s a lot to juggle on your own, and I’m sorry the last trip left you feeling that way. You’re not being difficult — these are real problems, and solving them is part of my job today.
model.why: Validates without judgement and makes the barriers part of the plan

model.text: I just thought if it’s a sprain…

I’ll be honest with you. Growing pains never stop a child walking, and there’s no injury to explain a sprain. A child who won’t put any weight on a leg, and has a temperature, needs to be examined and have a blood test today — because we have to rule out an infection in the hip joint or bone.
model.why: Rejects the unsafe label and names septic arthritis in plain words

model.text: An infection in the joint? From a cold?

Most likely this is an irritable hip after his cold, which settles by itself. But a joint infection looks the same at first, and it can damage the joint quickly if it’s missed. The only safe way to tell them apart is an examination, bloods and possibly a scan. I can’t do that over video, and neither of us should guess.
model.why: Shares the differential honestly and explains why it must be same day

model.text: Okay. When you put it like that.

Here’s what I suggest. I’ll phone the children’s team at the hospital now and ask them to expect him, so you go straight to them rather than sitting in the main waiting room. Now the practical side — is there anyone who could have the little one, or drive you?
model.why: Problem-solves the barriers inside the clinical plan

model.text: My neighbour might. Or I could get a taxi and take them both.

Either is fine — a taxi with both children is completely okay. If you truly can’t get there, ring me back straight away and we’ll arrange transport, because getting there is not optional today. And for work, you are entitled to time off to deal with an emergency involving your child.
model.why: Makes attendance certain and gives a fallback route

model.text: Right. I didn’t know that about work.
Carry him, don’t let him walk on it, and you can give him paracetamol for comfort — the usual dose for his age on the bottle.
model.why: Practical interim advice while awaiting assessment

model.text: If before you get there he becomes floppy, very sleepy, breathing fast, or you see a rash that doesn’t fade when you press a glass on it — ring 999. I’ll ring the hospital now, and I’ll call you this afternoon to check he’s been seen.
model.why: Specific 999 triggers and a named follow-up call

model.text: Okay. Thank you. I feel bad I nearly didn’t bother.
You did bother — you rang, and you’re doing right by him. Just so I know it’s clear: what’s the plan from here?
model.why: Removes guilt and checks understanding with teach-back

model.text: Neighbour or taxi, go straight to the children’s unit, carry him, Calpol. 999 if he goes floppy or gets a rash. You’ll ring me later.

social.t: No car, a younger sibling at home and work commitments are real barriers, not neglect. Plan childcare, transport and a direct route to the children’s team as part of the clinical management.
A long wait that ended in “it’s nothing” makes parents reluctant to return. Phoning ahead so the child is expected, and saying why today is different, rebuilds trust.

legal.t: Employees have a statutory right to reasonable unpaid time off to deal with an emergency involving a dependant (Employment Rights Act 1996, s57A). Telling her this can remove a barrier to attending.

NICE CG89: consider maltreatment where an injury or limp lacks an adequate explanation. Asking about mechanism is routine; no concern arises from this history as given, but the examining team should look for bruising.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice 2024 expects doctors to recognise the limits of their competence and of the consultation format. A child who will not weight-bear cannot be examined over video, so face-to-face assessment is needed.
Phone the paediatric team with the history, document the advice and the barriers discussed, and check the same day that the child was seen.

community.t: Neighbours, family or friends for sibling care; a taxi is appropriate for a child who must be carried. Health visitor or school nurse links can support a single parent afterwards.

redFlags: Complete refusal to weight-bear, especially with fever — septic arthritis or osteomyelitis until excluded, same-day assessment
Systemic features: lethargy, pallor, bruising, petechiae, night pain, weight loss — NICE NG12 leukaemia and bone sarcoma criteria
No adequate explanation for the limp or an inconsistent account — consider NAI (NICE CG89)
psychosocial: Single parent with a younger child, no car and work to get to
A previous long A&E wait that left her feeling foolish
Who can help today: neighbour, family, friend, taxi
ice: Idea: “It’s growing pains or he’s twisted it playing.”
Concern: getting to hospital with no car and a sibling, and wasting everyone’s time again
Expectation: sprain advice so she can manage at home

playbook.diagnosis: Acute refusal to weight-bear on the right leg in a febrile 5-year-old after a viral illness: septic arthritis of the hip or osteomyelitis must be excluded the same day. Transient synovitis is the most likely outcome but is a diagnosis of exclusion.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Finn’s hip or leg is inflamed. Most of the time after a cold that’s a harmless irritable hip that settles. But an infection in the joint can look exactly the same at first and needs treating fast, so he needs checking and a blood test today to tell them apart.”

management.reflectIce: “You were hoping for sprain advice because getting to hospital today feels impossible on your own. Let’s solve that together, because he does need to be seen today.”
management.psychosocial: Phone ahead to the paediatric team so she goes straight there; agree who has the sibling or take both by taxi; mention time off for dependants; offer transport help if there is no other route.
sharedPlan: Same-day paediatric assessment: examination, FBC, CRP, ESR, blood cultures and imaging (BOAST 2022)
Carry him, no weight-bearing, paracetamol for comfort (dose per BNFC)
Transport and childcare agreed before the call ends
safetyNet: 999 if floppy, drowsy, breathing fast or a non-blanching rash appears
GP rings later today to confirm he was seen; review after discharge if transient synovitis is diagnosed and it does not settle

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed in two opposite ways: colluding with a home label because the parent asked for one, or ordering her to A&E without hearing why she can’t get there. The marks sit in finding the fever and then getting Finn seen.

items.fail: Giving sprain or growing-pains advice with review tomorrow.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Refusal to weight-bear with possible fever needs same-day assessment (BOAST 2022).
items.fix: Say it plainly: “Growing pains never stop a child walking — he needs checking today.”

items.fail: Accepting “he feels a bit warm” and moving on.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Fever is the single fact that changes the urgency.
items.fix: Ask her to take his temperature while you wait, and say why it matters.

items.fail: Treating the video view as an examination and reassuring on what the camera shows.
items.why: Hip range of movement, tenderness and bruising cannot be assessed remotely; false reassurance is unsafe.
items.fix: Use the camera to observe posture and willingness to move, then say clearly that he needs to be examined in person.

items.fail: Telling her she must go to A&E and ending the call.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” Her barrier is practical; without solving it, Finn may not arrive.
items.fix: “What makes going in hard today?” — then plan childcare, transport and a direct route with her.

items.fail: Asking about injuries in a way that sounds accusing, or skipping the question entirely.
items.why: Either loses her trust or misses NAI. The question must be routine and neutral.
items.fix: “Any fall, knock or rough play in the last few days, at home, school or with anyone else?”

items.fail: “Come back if he gets worse” with no named symptoms and no check that he was seen.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no follow-up are standard failing feedback statements.
items.fix: Name the 999 triggers, phone ahead, and promise a call later today to confirm he was assessed.

timeMap.d: She opens with the sprain request and “I don’t want to drag him to A&E”. Let her finish; both halves matter.
Any weight at all? Get the temperature taken now. Systemic features, pallor, bruising, rash, mechanism. Observe the leg on camera without calling it an examination.
Why A&E feels impossible: single parent, sibling, no car, work, last wasted trip. Validate before explaining.
Growing pains never stop a child walking. Fever plus refusal to weight-bear means excluding joint infection today. Phone the paediatric team; solve transport and childcare with her.
999 triggers, interim analgesia, GP call later today. Teach-back of the plan.

wordPics.fail: Gives sprain advice or accepts “growing pains”; never finds out whether he is febrile; treats the video view as an examination; lectures or judges her about A&E; no same-day assessment and no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Recognises non-weight-bearing as a red flag; gets the temperature measured; names septic arthritis and arranges same-day assessment; asks about injury; gives basic safety-netting.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: draws out the single-parent, transport and childcare barriers and solves them inside the plan; phones ahead so she is expected; lifts the embarrassment about the last visit; screens for malignancy and NAI neutrally; confirms attendance with a same-day call and teach-back.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably just growing pains — rest, ice and Calpol, and see how he is tomorrow.”
avoid.instead: “Growing pains never stop a child walking. He needs to be examined today.”
avoid.why: A home label for a febrile child who will not weight-bear is the classic unsafe Tasks fail.

avoid.dont: “You really need to take him to A&E — it’s your responsibility.”
avoid.instead: “Getting there sounds hard today. Tell me what’s in the way, and let’s sort it together.”
avoid.why: Judgement loses her; problem-solving gets Finn seen and earns Relating marks.

avoid.dont: “From what I can see on the video, the hip looks fine.”
avoid.instead: “The video helps me see how he’s holding it, but I can’t examine a hip over a camera.”
avoid.why: Presenting video observation as an examination is false reassurance.

Could you lie him down and turn the camera to his legs? Let me see if the leg looks swollen or red, and whether he’ll let you move the hip and knee gently. Stop if it hurts him.
SCA_MODELS.why: Uses video to observe, without treating it as an examination

SCA_MODELS.text: He’s holding it bent and turned out a bit. He screams if I try to straighten it.
You said you don’t want to drag him to A&E. Can I ask what makes going in so hard today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Follows the cue to the hidden practical barrier

SCA_MODELS.text: It’s just me. I’ve got his little brother or sister here, no car, and I’m meant to be at work. Last time I sat in A&E for hours and they said it was nothing. I felt stupid.
That’s a lot to juggle on your own, and I’m sorry the last trip left you feeling that way. You’re not being difficult — these are real problems, and solving them is part of my job today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates without judgement and makes the barriers part of the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: I just thought if it’s a sprain…

I’ll be honest with you. Growing pains never stop a child walking, and there’s no injury to explain a sprain. A child who won’t put any weight on a leg, and has a temperature, needs to be examined and have a blood test today — because we have to rule out an infection in the hip joint or bone.
SCA_MODELS.why: Rejects the unsafe label and names septic arthritis in plain words

SCA_MODELS.text: An infection in the joint? From a cold?

Most likely this is an irritable hip after his cold, which settles by itself. But a joint infection looks the same at first, and it can damage the joint quickly if it’s missed. The only safe way to tell them apart is an examination, bloods and possibly a scan. I can’t do that over video, and neither of us should guess.
SCA_MODELS.why: Shares the differential honestly and explains why it must be same day

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. When you put it like that.

Here’s what I suggest. I’ll phone the children’s team at the hospital now and ask them to expect him, so you go straight to them rather than sitting in the main waiting room. Now the practical side — is there anyone who could have the little one, or drive you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Problem-solves the barriers inside the clinical plan

SCA_MODELS.text: My neighbour might. Or I could get a taxi and take them both.

Either is fine — a taxi with both children is completely okay. If you truly can’t get there, ring me back straight away and we’ll arrange transport, because getting there is not optional today. And for work, you are entitled to time off to deal with an emergency involving your child.
SCA_MODELS.why: Makes attendance certain and gives a fallback route

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. I didn’t know that about work.
Carry him, don’t let him walk on it, and you can give him paracetamol for comfort — the usual dose for his age on the bottle.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical interim advice while awaiting assessment

SCA_MODELS.text: If before you get there he becomes floppy, very sleepy, breathing fast, or you see a rash that doesn’t fade when you press a glass on it — ring 999. I’ll ring the hospital now, and I’ll call you this afternoon to check he’s been seen.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific 999 triggers and a named follow-up call

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Thank you. I feel bad I nearly didn’t bother.
You did bother — you rang, and you’re doing right by him. Just so I know it’s clear: what’s the plan from here?
SCA_MODELS.why: Removes guilt and checks understanding with teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Neighbour or taxi, go straight to the children’s unit, carry him, Calpol. 999 if he goes floppy or gets a rash. You’ll ring me later.

SCA_STEM.name: Finn
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: Mother requested a same-day video call this morning: woke limping, now refusing to walk on the right leg. Feels “a bit warm” to her; temperature not measured. No injury witnessed. No rash reported.
SCA_STEM.reason: Mother calling for advice. She hopes it is a sprain or growing pains that can be managed at home.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: BOAST: Management of children with acute musculoskeletal infection (BOA/BSCOS, 2022) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE CG89 · NICE NG254
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A child who suddenly refuses to bear weight has a serious cause until proven otherwise. With possible fever, septic arthritis or osteomyelitis must be excluded the same day; transient synovitis is a diagnosis made only after that.

points.h: Refusal to bear weight is a red flag
points.t: An acute limp or refusal to weight-bear needs examination in person the same day. Growing pains do not cause a limp or daytime refusal to walk, so they are never a safe label for this story.

BOAST 2022: children with suspected acute bone or joint infection are managed in hospital by orthopaedic and paediatric teams, with FBC, CRP, ESR and blood cultures, plain X-ray and then MRI as needed. Delay risks permanent joint damage. Consider sepsis in any unwell febrile child (NICE NG254, under 16s).

Kocher et al. 1999 (hospital-derived): fever above 38.5 °C, non-weight-bearing, ESR above 40 mm/h and WCC above 12 × 10⁹/L each raise the probability of septic arthritis of the hip. Two of the four can be judged on history; the other two need a blood test, which is why the assessment cannot happen at home.

At 5: transient synovitis (often after a viral illness), septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, Perthes disease, fracture or soft-tissue injury, reactive or juvenile idiopathic arthritis, malignancy and non-accidental injury. Slipped upper femoral epiphysis belongs to the older, heavier child.

NICE NG12: unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly — immediate specialist assessment for leukaemia. Pallor, persistent fatigue, unexplained fever, persistent infections, generalised lymphadenopathy, persistent or unexplained bone pain, unexplained bruising or bleeding — very urgent FBC (within 48 hours). Unexplained bone swelling or pain — consider a very urgent direct-access X-ray (within 48 hours) for bone sarcoma.

NICE CG89: consider maltreatment when an injury or limp has no adequate explanation or the account is inconsistent. Ask about the mechanism routinely and neutrally, and look for bruising when he is examined.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question first; let her tell the story; heard “won’t walk on it at all” and “I don’t want A&E” without cutting in.
Single parent, younger sibling, no car, work, previous long A&E wait — the practical reasons she is steering to home care.
Picked up “a bit warm” and “drag him to A&E”, got the temperature measured and explored the barrier.
Idea (sprain or growing pains), concern (getting there, feeling foolish again), expectation (home sprain advice).
Video used only to observe; in-person examination the same day with FBC, CRP, ESR, blood cultures and imaging in hospital (BOAST 2022).
Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis vs transient synovitis vs Perthes, injury, reactive arthritis, malignancy and NAI.
Established fever and complete refusal to bear weight; asked about systemic illness, pallor, bruising, rash and mechanism.
Stated clearly: acute non-weight-bearing with fever — joint or bone infection must be excluded today; transient synovitis only after that.
GP phones the paediatric team for same-day assessment; transport and childcare solved with her; interim analgesia.
Right to time off for dependants raised; sibling care planned; the previous poor A&E experience addressed.
999 triggers named (floppy, drowsy, fast breathing, non-blanching rash); GP call later the same day to confirm he was seen.

social.t: No car, a younger sibling at home and work commitments are real barriers, not neglect. Plan childcare, transport and a direct route to the children’s team as part of the clinical management.
A long wait that ended in “it’s nothing” makes parents reluctant to return. Phoning ahead so the child is expected, and saying why today is different, rebuilds trust.

legal.t: Employees have a statutory right to reasonable unpaid time off to deal with an emergency involving a dependant (Employment Rights Act 1996, s57A). Telling her this can remove a barrier to attending.

NICE CG89: consider maltreatment where an injury or limp lacks an adequate explanation. Asking about mechanism is routine; no concern arises from this history as given, but the examining team should look for bruising.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice 2024 expects doctors to recognise the limits of their competence and of the consultation format. A child who will not weight-bear cannot be examined over video, so face-to-face assessment is needed.
Phone the paediatric team with the history, document the advice and the barriers discussed, and check the same day that the child was seen.

community.t: Neighbours, family or friends for sibling care; a taxi is appropriate for a child who must be carried. Health visitor or school nurse links can support a single parent afterwards.

redFlags: Complete refusal to weight-bear, especially with fever — septic arthritis or osteomyelitis until excluded, same-day assessment
Systemic features: lethargy, pallor, bruising, petechiae, night pain, weight loss — NICE NG12 leukaemia and bone sarcoma criteria
No adequate explanation for the limp or an inconsistent account — consider NAI (NICE CG89)
psychosocial: Single parent with a younger child, no car and work to get to
A previous long A&E wait that left her feeling foolish
Who can help today: neighbour, family, friend, taxi
ice: Idea: “It’s growing pains or he’s twisted it playing.”
Concern: getting to hospital with no car and a sibling, and wasting everyone’s time again
Expectation: sprain advice so she can manage at home

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Acute refusal to weight-bear on the right leg in a febrile 5-year-old after a viral illness: septic arthritis of the hip or osteomyelitis must be excluded the same day. Transient synovitis is the most likely outcome but is a diagnosis of exclusion.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Finn’s hip or leg is inflamed. Most of the time after a cold that’s a harmless irritable hip that settles. But an infection in the joint can look exactly the same at first and needs treating fast, so he needs checking and a blood test today to tell them apart.”

management.reflectIce: “You were hoping for sprain advice because getting to hospital today feels impossible on your own. Let’s solve that together, because he does need to be seen today.”
management.psychosocial: Phone ahead to the paediatric team so she goes straight there; agree who has the sibling or take both by taxi; mention time off for dependants; offer transport help if there is no other route.
sharedPlan: Same-day paediatric assessment: examination, FBC, CRP, ESR, blood cultures and imaging (BOAST 2022)
Carry him, no weight-bearing, paracetamol for comfort (dose per BNFC)
Transport and childcare agreed before the call ends
safetyNet: 999 if floppy, drowsy, breathing fast or a non-blanching rash appears
GP rings later today to confirm he was seen; review after discharge if transient synovitis is diagnosed and it does not settle

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed in two opposite ways: colluding with a home label because the parent asked for one, or ordering her to A&E without hearing why she can’t get there. The marks sit in finding the fever and then getting Finn seen.

items.fail: Giving sprain or growing-pains advice with review tomorrow.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Refusal to weight-bear with possible fever needs same-day assessment (BOAST 2022).
items.fix: Say it plainly: “Growing pains never stop a child walking — he needs checking today.”

items.fail: Accepting “he feels a bit warm” and moving on.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Fever is the single fact that changes the urgency.
items.fix: Ask her to take his temperature while you wait, and say why it matters.

items.fail: Treating the video view as an examination and reassuring on what the camera shows.
items.why: Hip range of movement, tenderness and bruising cannot be assessed remotely; false reassurance is unsafe.
items.fix: Use the camera to observe posture and willingness to move, then say clearly that he needs to be examined in person.

items.fail: Telling her she must go to A&E and ending the call.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” Her barrier is practical; without solving it, Finn may not arrive.
items.fix: “What makes going in hard today?” — then plan childcare, transport and a direct route with her.

items.fail: Asking about injuries in a way that sounds accusing, or skipping the question entirely.
items.why: Either loses her trust or misses NAI. The question must be routine and neutral.
items.fix: “Any fall, knock or rough play in the last few days, at home, school or with anyone else?”

items.fail: “Come back if he gets worse” with no named symptoms and no check that he was seen.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no follow-up are standard failing feedback statements.
items.fix: Name the 999 triggers, phone ahead, and promise a call later today to confirm he was assessed.
